who2021aqg.title: WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide
who2021aqg.container: World Health Organization, Geneva (ISBN 9789240034228 electronic; 9789240034211 print)
who2021aqg.supports: Table 0.1 of the guideline document itself gives the 2021 AQG levels as PM2.5 5 ug/m3 (annual) and 15 ug/m3 (24-hour); PM10 15 ug/m3 (annual) and 45 ug/m3 (24-hour); 24-hour values are the 99th percentile (i.e. 3-4 exceedance days per year).

burnett2018gemm.title: Global estimates of mortality associated with long-term exposure to outdoor fine particulate matter
burnett2018gemm.container: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
burnett2018gemm.supports: The Global Exposure Mortality Model (GEMM), built from 41 cohorts in 16 countries, predicts 8.9 million (95% CI 7.5-10.3) deaths in 2015 attributable to outdoor PM2.5, 120% larger than the risk function used in the GBD (4.0 million; 95% CI 3.3-4.8).

lelieveld2015nature.title: The contribution of outdoor air pollution sources to premature mortality on a global scale
lelieveld2015nature.supports: Using a global atmospheric chemistry model, outdoor air pollution (mostly PM2.5) is calculated to lead to 3.3 (95% CI 1.61-4.81) million premature deaths per year worldwide, predominantly in Asia.

johnston2012lfs.title: Estimated global mortality attributable to smoke from landscape fires
johnston2012lfs.supports: Principal estimate of average mortality attributable to landscape-fire-smoke exposure was 339,000 deaths annually (interquartile range of sensitivity analyses 260,000-600,000), with Southeast Asia (110,000) among the most affected regions; estimated annual mortality was 262,000 during La Nina versus 532,000 during El Nino.

koplitz2016erl.title: Public health impacts of the severe haze in Equatorial Asia in September-October 2015: demonstration of a new framework for informing fire management strategies to reduce downwind smoke exposure
koplitz2016erl.supports: The authors estimate that haze in 2015 resulted in 100 300 excess deaths across Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, more than double those of the 2006 event, with much of the increase due to fires in Indonesia's South Sumatra Province.

kunii2002haze.title: The 1997 haze disaster in Indonesia: its air quality and health effects
kunii2002haze.supports: After interviewing 543 people and conducting lung-function tests, more than 90% of respondents had respiratory symptoms, and PM10 and CO reached 'very unhealthy' and 'hazardous' PSI levels during the 1997 Indonesia haze.

barkjohn2021purpleair.title: Development and application of a United States-wide correction for PM2.5 data collected with the PurpleAir sensor
barkjohn2021purpleair.supports: Raw PurpleAir data overestimate PM2.5 concentrations by about 40% in most parts of the US under typical ambient and smoke-impacted conditions, and a linear regression with a relative-humidity term reduces much of this bias.

mueller2020bb.title: Ambient particulate matter and biomass burning: an ecological time series study of respiratory and cardiovascular hospital visits in northern Thailand
mueller2020bb.supports: Using 2014-2017 northern Thailand outpatient data, same-day PM10 was associated with chronic lower respiratory disease visits (IRR 1.020, 95% CI 1.012-1.028) and cerebrovascular disease visits (IRR 1.020, 95% CI 1.004-1.035), with no association for ischaemic heart disease (IRR 0.994, 95% CI 0.974-1.014); PM10 peaked in March, coinciding with peak biomass burning.

uttajug2024fire.title: Effects of Coexposure to Air Pollution from Vegetation Fires and Extreme Heat on Mortality in Upper Northern Thailand
uttajug2024fire.supports: In Upper Northern Thailand all-cause mortality risk increased by 0.9% (95% CI 0.1-1.8) per 10 ug/m3 increase in same-day vegetation-fire PM2.5 and by 12.8% (95% CI 10.5-15.1) on extreme-heat (90th percentile) days, with no interactive effect.

sapbamrer2024copd.title: Decadal Trends in Ambient Air Pollutants and Their Association with COPD and Lung Cancer in Upper Northern Thailand: 2013–2022
sapbamrer2024copd.supports: In upper northern Thailand 2013-2022, during haze periods COPD fatality and re-admission rates rose significantly (mean difference 0.43 and 4.23 per 1000 cases, p<0.001) while lung cancer fatality was higher without statistical significance; PM2.5 exceeded air quality standards from January to April.

chantaraprachoom2024nation.title: A Nation-by-Nation Assessment of the Contribution of Southeast Asian Open Biomass Burning to PM2.5 in Thailand Using the Community Multiscale Air Quality-Integrated Source Apportionment Method Model
chantaraprachoom2024nation.supports: CMAQ-ISAM simulations for 2019 show open biomass burning substantially impacts PM2.5 in Thailand's Upper Northern Region, with Myanmar the major contributor in the west and central sub-regions and domestic burning the major contributor in the east during peak months; transboundary transport from Myanmar also raised Bangkok PM2.5 in March-April.

amnuaylojaroen2020lrt.title: Long Range Transport of Southeast Asian PM2.5 Pollution to Northern Thailand during High Biomass Burning Episodes
amnuaylojaroen2020lrt.supports: WRF-HYSPLIT analysis found Burma accounted for 37% of all Southeast Asian hotspot locations in March, and monsoon flow can bring pollutants from Burma and Laos toward northern Thailand in March, likely contributing to high PM2.5 there.

song2022bbnt.title: Is biomass burning always a dominant contributor of fine aerosols in upper northern Thailand?
song2022bbnt.supports: Radiocarbon and organic-marker source apportionment at Chiang Mai sites in 2018 found biomass-burning-derived OC was 65.5 +/- 5.8% (urban) and 79.9 +/- 7.6% (rural) of total carbon in the high burning season versus 39.1 +/- 7.9% and 42.8 +/- 4.6% in the low season.

lee2017lowvis.title: Biomass burning aerosols and the low-visibility events in Southeast Asia
lee2017lowvis.supports: Fire aerosols were responsible for nearly all very-low-visibility (<7 km) events in Southeast Asia and up to 39% of low-visibility (<10 km) events in Bangkok; mainland Southeast Asian burning accounts for 99% of fire-produced PM2.5 in Bangkok.

marks2022transbdry.title: A transboundary political ecology of air pollution: Slow violence on Thailand's margins
marks2022transbdry.supports: The authors argue that administrative fragmentation and the protection of vested economic interests by Thai business and political elites have compromised transboundary governance of the air in Thailand, and recommend legislation centred on cross-sectoral and cross-jurisdictional cooperation.

gu2024seasource.title: Source emission contributions to particulate matter and ozone, and their health impacts in Southeast Asia
gu2024seasource.supports: Species-tagged modelling attributes about 900 thousand premature deaths per year in Southeast Asia to air pollution, 77% from local emissions and 23% from transboundary air pollution, with TAP impacts especially adverse in border regions and in Laos.

lin2013overview.title: An overview of regional experiments on biomass burning aerosols and related pollutants in Southeast Asia: From BASE-ASIA and the Dongsha Experiment to 7-SEAS
lin2013overview.supports: The overview summarises the BASE-ASIA (2006) and 7-SEAS/Dongsha (2010) spring campaigns in northern Southeast Asia and a 28-paper special issue characterising biomass-burning aerosols and related pollutants near source and in sink regions.

reid2013review.title: Observing and understanding the Southeast Asian aerosol system by remote sensing: An initial review and analysis for the Seven Southeast Asian Studies (7SEAS) program
reid2013review.supports: The review (written for the 7SEAS programme) describes Southeast Asia as one of the most complex aerosol systems in the world, identifies biomass burning as its most studied aerosol issue, and concludes that satellite aerosol data products diverge greatly owing to known artifacts.

reid2012mc.title: Multi-scale meteorological conceptual analysis of observed active fire hotspot activity and smoke optical depth in the Maritime Continent
reid2012mc.supports: MODIS hotspot and aerosol-assimilation analysis for the Maritime Continent finds ENSO is the largest factor in burning, enhanced also by El Nino Modoki, while the Madden-Julian Oscillation largely controls when visible burning occurs.

marlier2013elnino.title: El Niño and health risks from landscape fire emissions in southeast Asia
marlier2013elnino.supports: For 1997-2006 in Southeast Asia, during strong El Nino years fires contribute up to 200 ug/m3 annual-average PM2.5 near fire sources, about 200 additional days per year exceeding the WHO 50 ug/m3 24-h interim target, and an estimated 10,800 (6,800-14,300) person (~2%) annual increase in regional adult cardiovascular mortality.

nurdiati2022enso.title: Joint Pattern Analysis of Forest Fire and Drought Indicators in Southeast Asia Associated with ENSO and IOD
nurdiati2022enso.supports: The authors report that Cambodia, Myanmar and Thailand showed a similar result with less than a 25% increase in hotspot severity from normal to El Nino, positive IOD, or El Nino-positive IOD years, compared with more than 72% (Kalimantan) and 89% (South Sumatra) increases during the strong 2015 El Nino.

marvin2024bbuncert.title: Uncertainties from biomass burning aerosols in air quality models obscure public health impacts in Southeast Asia
marvin2024bbuncert.supports: GEOS-Chem for March and September 2014 underestimates regional aerosol burden relative to satellite AOD (20-52%) and ground PM (up to 54%), especially in early burning season (March); sensitivity modifications improve March agreement to within 31%.

giglio2016c6.title: The collection 6 MODIS active fire detection algorithm and fire products
giglio2016c6.supports: Describes the MODIS Collection 6 active-fire algorithm; MOD14 Collection 6 daytime global commission error was 1.2% versus 2.4% in Collection 5, with reduced omission errors over large fires and reduced false-alarm rates in tropical ecosystems.

schroeder2014viirs.title: The New VIIRS 375 m active fire detection data product: Algorithm description and initial assessment
schroeder2014viirs.supports: The VIIRS 375 m active-fire algorithm showed small, variable commission errors (<1.2%) for nominal-confidence fire pixels and detected 3x (day) and 25x (night) more fire pixels than the VIIRS 750 m baseline product.

davies2009firms.title: Fire Information for Resource Management System: Archiving and Distributing MODIS Active Fire Data
davies2009firms.container: IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
davies2009firms.supports: Describes FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), a NASA-funded system that delivers MODIS active-fire data via Internet mapping services and customised e-mail alerts to users in more than 90 countries.

holben1998aeronet.title: AERONET—A Federated Instrument Network and Data Archive for Aerosol Characterization
holben1998aeronet.supports: Describes AERONET as a NASA-initiated remote-sensing aerosol monitoring network with open-access database, centralized processing, near-real-time processing, and discusses radiometer precision/accuracy and database access.

giles2019aeronetv3.title: Advancements in the Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET) Version 3 database – automated near-real-time quality control algorithm with improved cloud screening for Sun photometer aerosol optical depth (AOD) measurements
giles2019aeronetv3.supports: AERONET Version 3 provides fully automatic cloud screening and instrument-anomaly quality control for near-real-time and reprocessed data (database reprocessed in 2018), with Level 2.0 AOD available within a month of post-field calibration.

schuster2006angstrom.title: Angstrom exponent and bimodal aerosol size distributions
schuster2006angstrom.supports: The Angstrom exponent is often used as a qualitative indicator of aerosol particle size, with values greater than 2 indicating small particles associated with combustion byproducts and values less than 1 indicating large particles such as sea salt and dust.

angstrom1929dust.title: On the Atmospheric Transmission of Sun Radiation and on Dust in the Air
angstrom1929dust.supports: Original source of the wavelength power-law (Angstrom exponent) description of atmospheric extinction by dust; only the bibliographic record (Geografiska Annaler 11(2):156-166) was verified, no abstract exists.

inness2019cams.title: The CAMS reanalysis of atmospheric composition
inness2019cams.supports: The CAMS reanalysis (ECMWF; 2003-2016 at the time, ~80 km resolution) assimilates satellite CO, NO2, AOD and ozone retrievals and has smaller biases than the previous MACC and CAMS-interim reanalyses against independent ozone, CO, NO2 and AOD observations.

stein2015hysplit.title: NOAA’s HYSPLIT Atmospheric Transport and Dispersion Modeling System
stein2015hysplit.container: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society
stein2015hysplit.supports: Describes the evolution of NOAA's HYSPLIT trajectory and dispersion modelling system over 30 years and highlights applications including smoke from wild fires.

tan2023camsmalaysia.title: Assessment of Malaysia-wide PM2.5 Forecasts from a Global Model
tan2023camsmalaysia.supports: CAMS global atmospheric composition forecast (cycle 46r1) PM2.5 evaluated against hourly Malaysian observations 2018-2020 performed generally weaker (CSI = 31%, R2 = 0.36) than reported elsewhere (CSI = 20-54%, R2 = 0.32-0.79), missed local spatiotemporal variation but better captured the regional 2019 transboundary haze episode; authors recommend bias-correction.

wu2020camsforecast.title: Validation and Calibration of CAMS PM2.5 Forecasts Using In Situ PM2.5 Measurements in China and United States
wu2020camsforecast.supports: CAMS PM2.5 forecasts for 2017-2018 in China showed mean correlation 0.31-0.45 and RMSE 38-83 ug/m3 (US: 0.24-0.42; 8.30-16.76 ug/m3) as lead time grew from 3 h to 120 h, with large spatially varied modelling biases; a random-forest bias correction substantially reduced them.

ali2022camsmerra.title: Accuracy assessment of CAMS and MERRA-2 reanalysis PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations over China
ali2022camsmerra.supports: Against 1,675 Chinese monitoring stations (2014-2020), CAMS significantly OVERestimates PM2.5 and PM10 over most regions (especially urban and desert areas), and both CAMS and MERRA-2 substantially underestimate the lowest concentrations over the Tibetan Plateau and Qinghai.

koschmieder1924.title: Theorie der horizontalen Sichtweite
koschmieder1924.container: Beitraege zur Physik der freien Atmosphaere
koschmieder1924.supports: Original theory of horizontal visibility (Part I) underlying the visibility-extinction (Koschmieder) relation; only the bibliographic record was verified, no abstract exists.

ye2023visibility.title: Consistency and Discrepancy between Visibility and PM2.5 Measurements: Potential Application of Visibility Observation to Air Quality Study
ye2023visibility.supports: For 2016-2018 China, the Spearman correlation between PM2.5 and visibility-derived surface extinction coefficient was significant at most stations (national median rho = 0.67 in winter), with lower rho (<0.4) in the cleanest regions, partly attributed to the ~30 km maximum visibility threshold.

he2011dcp.title: Single Image Haze Removal Using Dark Channel Prior
he2011dcp.container: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
he2011dcp.supports: Proposes the dark channel prior, based on the observation that most local patches in outdoor haze-free images contain some pixels with very low intensity in at least one colour channel, enabling estimation of haze thickness and a depth map from a single image.

liu2016particle.title: Particle Pollution Estimation Based on Image Analysis
liu2016particle.supports: Six image features extracted from outdoor images of Beijing, Shanghai and Phoenix, combined with sun position, date, time, geographic and weather data, were used to predict PM2.5 index, and the abstract reports 'good prediction' with different features of different significance (no numeric accuracy in abstract).

shin2022camera.title: Estimation of Aerosol Extinction Coefficient Using Camera Images and Application in Mass Extinction Efficiency Retrieval
shin2022camera.supports: Extinction coefficient computed from commercial-camera RGB pixels correlated with PM2.5 mass concentration at R2 = 0.7 (higher than with visibility data), despite a limited mass range; derived mass extinction efficiency was (10.8 +/- 6.9) m2/g, higher than earlier Northeast Asia values, which the authors flag as needing further long-term study.

laohakiat2023bkk.title: Visually Estimating and Forecasting PM2.5 Levels Using Hybrid Architecture Deep Neural Network
laohakiat2023bkk.supports: Hourly sky/building photographs from a high-rise in Bangkok with nearest-station ground truth: a hybrid CNN-LSTM model outperformed conventional CNN models by 5% (estimation) and 30% (forecasting).

wu2024surveillance.title: Time-Series Forecasting of PM2.5 and PM10 Concentrations Based on the Integration of Surveillance Images
wu2024surveillance.supports: A VGG16-LSTM model integrating surveillance images with numerical data forecast PM2.5 and PM10 for 2021 Shanghai with R2 0.9459/0.9045 and RMSE 4.79/11.51 ug/m3; transfer to two Kaohsiung stations gave average R2 0.9728/0.9365 for PM2.5/PM10; the authors list expanding datasets and optimising architectures as future work.

giordano2021lowcost.title: From low-cost sensors to high-quality data: A summary of challenges and best practices for effectively calibrating low-cost particulate matter mass sensors
giordano2021lowcost.supports: Low-cost PM sensors are subject to biases and calibration dependencies (meteorology, sensor age, aerosol source, composition, refractive index), corrected with methods from linear/quadratic models to machine learning, and the review sets out best practices for obtaining high-quality data.

dejchanchaiwong2023lcs.title: Seasonal Field Calibration of Low-Cost PM2.5 Sensors in Different Locations with Different Sources in Thailand
dejchanchaiwong2023lcs.supports: More than 1500 low-cost sensors are installed in Thailand; co-located with an FEM reference at Chiang Mai (north), Bangkok and Ubon Ratchathani, PMS7003 performance was acceptable in Chiang Mai (dry season) and Ubon Ratchathani after multiple-regression calibration (slope 0.829-0.945, R2 0.880-0.934, RMSE 4.3-5.1 ug/m3), while errors were mainly at low concentrations and high humidity and sensors underestimated in congested Bangkok.

theerawasttanasiri2024visual.title: Accuracy of estimating a human-sighted visual range for short-term particulate matter concentration in Chiang Mai, Thailand
theerawasttanasiri2024visual.container: International Journal of Public Health Asia Pacific
theerawasttanasiri2024visual.supports: In Chiang Mai (April-May 2018, 25 districts with DustBoy devices), trained health staff's human-sighted visual range reached 79.21% accuracy for PM10 but only 26.49% for PM2.5 (classified 'not useful'), and was ineffective at twilight, on rainy/cloudy days or with humidity >65%.

glahn1972mos.title: The Use of Model Output Statistics (MOS) in Objective Weather Forecasting
glahn1972mos.supports: Original paper introducing Model Output Statistics (MOS) for objective weather forecasting (J. Appl. Meteor. 11(8):1203-1211); only bibliographic record checked (no abstract in Crossref).

jolliffe2012forecastverification.title: Forecast Verification: A Practitioner's Guide in Atmospheric Science
jolliffe2012forecastverification.supports: Standard reference text on forecast verification methods in atmospheric science (edited volume, 2nd edition; ISBN 978-0-470-66071-3 hardcover, 978-1-119-96107-9 e-book).

wilks2019stats.title: Statistical Methods in the Atmospheric Sciences
wilks2019stats.supports: Standard textbook on statistical methods in the atmospheric sciences (4th edition, 2019).

wilson1927.title: Probable Inference, the Law of Succession, and Statistical Inference
wilson1927.container: Journal of the American Statistical Association
wilson1927.supports: Origin of the Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion (JASA 22(158):209-212); only bibliographic record checked.

efron1979bootstrap.title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
efron1979bootstrap.supports: Original bootstrap paper (Annals of Statistics 7(1):1-26); only bibliographic record checked.

spearman1904.title: The Proof and Measurement of Association between Two Things
spearman1904.supports: Original source of the rank correlation coefficient (Am. J. Psychol. 15(1)); only the bibliographic record was checked.

brown2001binomial.title: Interval Estimation for a Binomial Proportion
brown2001binomial.supports: Statistical Science 16(2):101-133 review of interval estimation for a binomial proportion (optional extra for Wilson interval justification); only bibliographic record checked.

authors: Chiang Mai University Climate Change Data Center (CCDC)
cmuccdc.title: CMU CCDC website - DustBoy PM2.5 network pages (status, API, installation guide)
cmuccdc.supports: The CCDC site hosts DustBoy menus (What is DustBoy, DustBoy status, DustBoy API, installation guide, sensor performance and USEPA calibration reports) and PM2.5 data pages.

saberian2017alerts.title: Alerts work! Air quality warnings and cycling
saberian2017alerts.supports: Using administrative cycling data from Sydney, an air quality alert reduces cycling by 14-35% (a substantial behavioural response), robust across specifications, and the authors also find evidence of 'alert fatigue'.

janke2014avoidance.title: Air pollution, avoidance behaviour and children's respiratory health: Evidence from England
janke2014avoidance.supports: With English local-authority panel data, there is evidence of avoidance behaviour in response to air pollution warnings for children's asthma admissions (where avoidance is less costly), but ignoring avoidance does not produce a statistically significant underestimate of the health effect of air pollution.

janjua2021cochrane.title: Individual-level interventions to reduce personal exposure to outdoor air pollution and their effects on people with long-term respiratory conditions
janjua2021cochrane.supports: Cochrane review found conflicting evidence on health-care usage from three studies of air pollution alerts (one non-randomised trial of 35 participants reporting increased emergency attendances; two randomised trials of 1553 participants reporting little to no difference), rated very uncertain, and inconsistent effects of alerts and education on adherence; the authors conclude lack of evidence limits conclusions.

riley2021communicate.title: How do we effectively communicate air pollution to change public attitudes and behaviours? A review
riley2021communicate.supports: A systematic review of 37 studies of air-pollution communication campaigns found avoidance behaviour (e.g. reducing outdoor activity) was most commonly studied, that actionable, targeted localized information and positive framing are likely to help, and that smartphones enable targeted engagement but care is needed not to transfer responsibility from authorities to individuals.

mahajan2022citizen.title: Translating citizen-generated air quality data into evidence for shaping policy
mahajan2022citizen.supports: Reviews citizen-science air-quality monitoring initiatives in Asia, Africa, Europe and Latin America and finds little research on how citizen-generated data feed evidence-based policymaking; proposes a methodology combining scientific evidence, participation and deliberation.

morawska2018lowcost.title: Applications of low-cost sensing technologies for air quality monitoring and exposure assessment: How far have they gone?
morawska2018lowcost.supports: A literature review of low-cost sensing found no clear answer on fitness for purpose (lack of manufacturer performance specifications and agreed minimum targets), and that about 30% of 17 large applied projects were commercial and/or crowd-funded, signalling a paradigm change from monitoring led by government organisations.

castell2017lowcost.title: Can commercial low-cost sensor platforms contribute to air quality monitoring and exposure estimates?
castell2017lowcost.supports: Evaluating 24 identical units of a commercial low-cost sensor platform against CEN reference analysers showed performance varies by unit, time and conditions; such platforms present low accuracy for regulatory or health purposes but can provide relative and aggregated information on air quality (e.g. awareness raising).

authors: Tam Roy Pao project (site hosted by the Hydro-Informatics Institute)
tamroypao.title: Tam Roy Pao - open burning / burn-scar monitoring system
tamroypao.supports: The site (Thai) states the system was developed under the project 'research and development of a system to process, report and monitor open burning areas using high-resolution satellite imagery', funded by a National Research Council of Thailand and Kasetsart University research-promotion grant for B.E. 2567 (2024), and provides a dashboard for 8 northern provinces, a web map, monthly/seasonal burn-scar downloads (CSV, GeoTIFF, TMS, API), 7-day 20 m burn-scar products (77 Sentinel-2 grid tiles) and agricultural burn areas split by rice, sugarcane, maize and mixed crops.

suwanprasit2024obia.title: Mapping burned areas in Thailand using Sentinel-2 imagery and OBIA techniques
suwanprasit2024obia.supports: Sentinel-2A (10 m) with object-based image analysis mapped burned areas in five Chiang Mai districts from a 27 Feb 2018 image and was 85.2% accurate against 500 random burned points from an existing burned-area dataset.

authors: Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA)
gistda_fire.title: Disaster Platform - Fire (hotspot service)
gistda_fire.supports: GISTDA's Disaster Platform (page title 'Fire | Disaster Platform', described as a decision-support system for disaster management) offers a fire view with province/district/sub-district selectors alongside flood and drought views.

nasa_firms.title: Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS)
nasa_firms.supports: NASA LANCE FIRMS web portal exists and distributes active-fire data (page title 'NASA | LANCE | FIRMS'); detailed dataset claims not extracted.

aathp2002text.title: ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (signed Kuala Lumpur, 10 June 2002; in force 25 November 2003)
aathp2002text.supports: Official text of the Agreement: Article 3(1) recognises the Parties' sovereign right to exploit their own resources pursuant to their own environmental and developmental policies and the responsibility to ensure activities within their jurisdiction do not harm other States; Article 29 provides entry into force on the sixtieth day after deposit of the sixth instrument; done at Kuala Lumpur on the tenth day of June 2002.

aathp_portal.title: ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (status and ratification table)
aathp_portal.supports: The official ASEAN Haze Portal table (as of 20 January 2015) gives date of ratification/approval and date of deposit: Thailand 10 September 2003 / 26 September 2003; Indonesia 14 October 2014 / 20 January 2015; Myanmar 5 March 2003 / 17 March 2003 (also Brunei 27 Feb/23 Apr 2003; Cambodia 24 Apr/9 Nov 2006; Lao PDR 19 Dec 2004/13 Jul 2005; Malaysia 3 Dec 2002/18 Feb 2003; Philippines 1 Feb/4 Mar 2010; Singapore 13/14 Jan 2003; Viet Nam 24 Mar/29 May 2003); signed 10 June 2002 in Kuala Lumpur; ratified by all ASEAN Member States; ASEAN Secretariat serves as Interim ACC.

aseanhub_indonesia_ratification.title: Indonesia Deposits Instrument of Ratification of the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution
aseanhub_indonesia_ratification.container: ASEAN Environment Knowledge Hub (media release, 21 January 2015; Internet Archive copy)
aseanhub_indonesia_ratification.supports: On 20 January 2015 Indonesia deposited its instrument of ratification with the ASEAN Secretary-General (approved by Indonesia's Parliament through Law No. 26 Year 2014); the Agreement was signed on 10 June 2002 in Kuala Lumpur and entered into force on 25 November 2003.

haze_roadmap1.title: Roadmap on ASEAN Cooperation towards Transboundary Haze Pollution Control with Means of Implementation (2016-2020) (Haze-free Roadmap)
haze_roadmap1.supports: The first Haze-free Roadmap (2016-2020) was adopted at COP-12 on 11 August 2016 in Kuala Lumpur, with a vision of a Transboundary Haze-free ASEAN by 2020 and indicators including more days with good/moderate air quality, fewer hotspots below Alert Level 2, and a smaller transboundary haze area.

haze_roadmap2.title: Media Release: 17th ASEAN Ministerial Meeting on the Environment and 18th Meeting of the COP to the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (Vientiane, 23 August 2023)
haze_roadmap2.supports: The Meetings welcomed the adoption of the Second Roadmap on ASEAN Cooperation towards Transboundary Haze Pollution Control with Means of Implementation (Haze-free Roadmap) 2023-2030 and the Second ASEAN Peatland Management Strategy 2023-2030, endorsed the ASEAN Investment Framework for Haze-free Sustainable Land Management, and noted ASMC's assessment that Alert Level 3 was issued for the Mekong sub-region on 2 March 2023 and that Mekong-region hotspot count was ~57% higher in 2023 than 2022 over January-August.

asmc_portal.title: ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC)
asmc_portal.supports: ASMC was established in January 1993, is hosted by Meteorological Service Singapore (NEA), and is the designated body to monitor and assess land and forest fires and transboundary smoke haze affecting ASEAN, providing monthly weather and haze outlooks, satellite images, hotspot information, air quality information and fire danger rating.

tan2005athp.title: The ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution: Prospects for Compliance and Effectiveness in Post-Suharto Indonesia
tan2005athp.supports: The article (by Alan Khee-Jin Tan) examines the prospects for compliance with and effectiveness of the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution in post-Suharto Indonesia; only the bibliographic listing was verified (no abstract read).

heilmann2015athp.title: After Indonesia's Ratification: The ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution and its Effectiveness as a Regional Environmental Governance Tool
heilmann2015athp.container: Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs
heilmann2015athp.supports: Argues that Indonesia's January 2015 ratification will not be an immediate game changer because the agreement's mechanisms are too weak; it is designed according to the ASEAN way, a non-binding approach based on state sovereignty and non-intervention.

forsyth2014publicconcerns.title: Public concerns about transboundary haze: A comparison of Indonesia, Singapore, and Malaysia
forsyth2014publicconcerns.supports: Content analysis of 2,231 newspaper articles from Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia on the 1997, 2005 and 2013 haze crises shows coverage shifting from health/economic impacts toward blaming Indonesia for not ratifying the 2002 ASEAN agreement, and criticism of palm-oil investors and of ASEAN itself.

quah2002fires.title: Transboundary Pollution in Southeast Asia: The Indonesian Fires
quah2002fires.supports: World Development 30(3):429-441 'Transboundary pollution in Southeast Asia: The Indonesian fires' - indexed abstract text (via ASEAN Haze Portal/ADINET records) describes a transboundary haze problem with severe economic ramifications and proposes stakeholder-based cost sharing; abstract itself not read from publisher.

authors: Researcher at the Research Center for Society and Culture, Indonesian Institute of Sciences (P2KK-LIPI) Jakarta, Indonesia
nurhidayah2015intlaw.title: The Influence of International Law upon ASEAN Approaches in Addressing Transboundary Haze Pollution in Southeast Asia
nurhidayah2015intlaw.supports: Contemporary Southeast Asia 37(2):183-210 examines the influence of international law upon ASEAN approaches to transboundary haze pollution; abstract not available in Crossref/OpenAlex (only issue line).

hurley2020delayed.title: Delayed ratification in environmental regimes: Indonesia’s ratification of the ASEAN agreement on transboundary haze pollution
hurley2020delayed.supports: Indonesia's lawmakers unanimously ratified the AATHP on 16 September 2014; eight of ten member states had ratified by 2006 and nine by 2010; the negotiated AATHP was 'soft' and thus low-cost for domestic stakeholders, yet key domestic actors had little appetite to ratify and neighbours' pressure was limited until the 2010s.

varkkey2016haze.title: The Haze Problem in Southeast Asia: Palm Oil and Patronage
varkkey2016haze.supports: Monograph on Southeast Asia's haze problem; Crossref/Open Library confirm title (as 'The Haze Problem in Southeast Asia'), author Helena Varkkey, publisher Routledge/Taylor & Francis; content summary not read.

tdri2023pm25.title: Challenges in tackling PM2.5 crisis (TDRI Insight; first published in the Bangkok Post, 12 April 2023)
tdri2023pm25.supports: TDRI argues the haze problem is 'a deep-seated structural problem' of 'inert bureaucracy and silo culture', that the panel overseeing the PM2.5 crisis 'operates as an ad hoc body without any consistency', that agencies bargain with the Budget Bureau for their share, that provincial governors face rules barring them from taking budget from other departments, and that local agencies 'don't get a budget for PM2.5' (provincial budget fell from 48.6 billion baht in 2018 to 19.6 billion baht in 2020).

tei2022burning.title: Management and Reduction of Burning Practice in Agricultural Areas and Policy Recommendations to Tackle PM2.5 in Thailand (1st revised and updated edition, January 2022)
tei2022burning.container: Thailand Environment Institute Foundation; supported by Pure Earth, PCD (MoNRE), GAHP, UNEP, APCAP
tei2022burning.supports: The report states the Cabinet made particulate matter a National Agenda on 12 February 2019 and adopted the Action Plan to Drive the National Agenda on 1 October 2019 (via MoNRE, endorsed by the National Environment Board), assigns measures to several bodies (Ministries of Agriculture and Cooperatives, Finance, Industry and Energy, and the Bangkok Metropolitan Authority and provincial administrations) and lists a sub-committee on forest fire, smog and particulate pollution under the National Committee on Disaster Prevention and Relief.

akahoshi2024burning.title: The Prospects of Controlling Open Burning of Crop Residues in Thailand: A Quantitative Assessment of Implementation Barriers and Costs
akahoshi2024burning.supports: In a quantitative assessment of burning restrictions in Thailand's PM2.5 control plan, institutional/social barriers delay implementation more than technical/economic barriers, leaving about twice the PM2.5 emissions of an effectively implemented policy over 10-20 years; overcoming them costs about US$14 million a year (~70% of the US$21 million planned for burning control in 2026).

evrard2023becoming.title: Becoming a Crisis: Shifting Narratives of Seasonal Air Pollution in Northern Thailand (1996–2019)
evrard2023becoming.supports: Analysis of three Thai national newspapers over 25 years plus fieldwork shows the Chiang Mai 'haze crisis' narrative developed through debates over forest use, agro-capitalism and legitimate political power (a framing/politics paper, not an agency-mandate analysis).

mostafanezhad2025legible.title: Making air pollution legible: Environmental‐health data and the naturalization of the smoky season in Northern Thailand†
mostafanezhad2025legible.supports: Ethnographic work 2019-2024 argues that official data only partially support claims of worsening northern Thai haze, and that solutions are framed as technocratic challenges rather than restructuring of socioeconomic relations of production.

nec2022pm25std.title: Notification of the National Environment Board: Setting the standard of particulate matter not exceeding 2.5 microns in ambient air (signed 23 June 2022; Royal Gazette Vol. 139, Special Part 163 Ng, 8 July 2022, p. 21-22)
nec2022pm25std.container: Royal Gazette (copy hosted by Pollution Control Department, pcd.go.th)
nec2022pm25std.supports: The notification (Thai) repeals NEB Notification No. 36 (B.E. 2553) and sets the 24-hour PM2.5 standard at not more than 50 ug/m3 through 31 May 2023 and not more than 37.5 ug/m3 from 1 June 2023 onward, and an annual arithmetic mean of not more than 15 ug/m3; in force from the day after publication (9 July 2022); monitoring by FRM/FEM-equivalent methods including light scattering.

pcd2023aqi.title: Notification of the Pollution Control Department: Air Quality Index of Thailand B.E. 2566 (2023) (dated 16 May 2023; Royal Gazette Vol. 140, Special Part 157 Ng, 3 July 2023)
pcd2023aqi.supports: Thai AQI 2023 has five levels (0-25 very good, 26-50 good, 51-100 moderate, 101-200 beginning to affect health, 201+ affects health) with 24-h PM2.5 breakpoints 0-15.0, 15.1-25.0, 25.1-37.5, 37.6-75.0 and 75.1+ ug/m3 (PM10 24-h: 0-50, 51-80, 81-120, 121-180, 181+); AQI 100 equals the ambient standard; it repeals the PCD AQI notification of 24 September 2018.

cleanair_status.title: Thai MPs reject clean air changes for 20-member joint panel review (3 September 2026) [with Nation Thailand 17 September 2026 'Thailand faces mounting climate risks amid Clean Air Bill delay']
cleanair_status.supports: As of early-to-mid September 2026 the Clean Air Management Bill is NOT yet law: the House voted 414 to 2 to reject the Senate's amendments and the text went to a 20-member joint House-Senate committee (10 MPs, 10 senators); the 17 September 2026 article says it remains in the legislative process with no deadline.

iqair2026chiangmai_mar27.title: March 27, 2026: Chiang Mai among top 10 most polluted cities in the world
iqair2026chiangmai_mar27.supports: IQAir states 'Chiang Mai ranked as the most polluted major city in the world on Thursday night' (26 March 2026, AQI above 220) and that Chiang Mai's 2025 average PM2.5 was 18.2 ug/m3, 3.6 times the WHO annual guideline of 5 ug/m3.

iqair2026chiangmai_mar4.title: March 4, 2026: Chiang Mai among the top 10 most polluted cities during Thailand's burning season
iqair2026chiangmai_mar4.supports: IQAir states that on the morning of 4 March 2026 'Chiang Mai ranked 3rd among the most polluted major cities in the world' (AQI above 150), that its 2024 average PM2.5 was 26.4 ug/m3 (5.2 times the WHO annual guideline), and that the burning season runs January-April peaking in March.

iqair2025improved.title: Top 5 Asian cities with most improved air quality in 2025
iqair2025improved.container: IQAir newsroom (13 July 2026), citing the 2025 World Air Quality Report
iqair2025improved.supports: IQAir reports Chiang Mai's average annual PM2.5 fell from 26.4 ug/m3 in 2024 to 18.2 ug/m3 in 2025 (an 8.2 ug/m3 improvement).

sei2021thailand.title: Air quality in Thailand: Understanding the regulatory context (SEI working paper)
sei2021thailand.supports: The SEI desk review states that 'many disparate Ministries and agencies are involved with different mandates', that policies are owned and enforced by the agency under which the source falls with 'little integration across sectors', that local and provincial governments 'frequently lack the necessary data and mandate to take enforcement action', and that there is 'no overarching agency with a responsibility for clean air'; its policy table also records provincial authority (Public Disaster Prevention and Mitigation Act 2007) to prohibit burning for 60 days.

bran2022wrfchem.title: Surface PM2.5 mass concentrations during the dry season over northern Thailand: Sensitivity to model aerosol chemical schemes and the effects on regional meteorology
bran2022wrfchem.supports: For 15 March-15 April 2019 over northern Thailand (observed PM2.5 40-240 ug/m3), WRF-Chem with GOCART and MOSAIC aerosol schemes captured spatiotemporal variation but underestimated observed PM2.5 magnitudes by about 24% and 27%, respectively; EDGAR-HTAP anthropogenic emissions gave more realistic results than CAMS-GLOB-ANT in most regions.

sowden2024cams.title: An Evaluation of Ground-Level Concentrations of Aerosols and Criteria Pollutants Using the CAMS Reanalysis Dataset over the Himawari-8 Observational Area, Including China, Indonesia, and Australia (2016–2023)
sowden2024cams.supports: CAMS reanalysis evaluated for 2016-2023 over the Himawari-8 area (China, Indonesia, Australia): CAMS captures large-scale pollution episodes but discrepancies in ground-level concentrations are apparent, especially during short-term events with vertical aerosol stratification.
